intro: The third movement of Mahler’s Second Symphony, the “Resurrection”, is a scherzo based on his song about St Anthony preaching to the fish, who enjoy the sermon and change nothing. The strings play continuous running figures until the full orchestra reaches a climax in B♭ minor.

sections.label: A · Timpani strokes and running string figures
sections.mNote: Timpani strike G and C; the running figures begin.

sections.label: B · Bassoons, then trumpet melody
sections.mNote: Low phrases in the middle section lead to a brass melody.

sections.label: A′ · Strings resume the opening figures
sections.mNote: Short figures return beneath held wind and brass notes

sections.label: Dev · B♭-minor climax, brass and percussion
sections.mNote: Brass and percussion enter over the running strings.

sections.label: Coda · Cellos and basses resume the motion
sections.mNote: Held chords die away above the moving cellos and basses

cues.title: Opening, timpani and strings
cues.text: The timpani strike G and C. The strings then begin a continuous running figure, with short woodwind interjections above it. The heading asks for quietly flowing motion, and the string figures repeatedly turn back on themselves.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement III, opening. The dominant–tonic timpani and double ostinato are described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-3-in-ruhig-fliessender-bewegung-scherzo/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E♭ clarinet solo, mit Humor
cues.text: The E♭ clarinet enters over the continuous string figuration with a short solo, which Mahler marks mit Humor, with humour. It plays in its high, shrill register above the strings.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 82: the E♭ clarinet’s short solo carries the marking mit Humor (https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: St Anthony’s sermon to the fishes
cues.text: The scherzo shares its music with Mahler’s Wunderhorn song Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt. In the song, St Anthony finds his church empty and takes his sermon to the river, where the fish gather with their mouths open and enjoy every word. Afterwards the pike still steal and the carp still gorge themselves.
cues.evidence: The Wunderhorn poem Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt, whose music Mahler shares with this scherzo: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/wunderhorn-12/des-knaben-wunderhorn-12-songs-lied-6-des-antonius-von-padua-fischpredigt/

cues.title: Melody in bassoons and cellos
cues.text: Bassoons and cellos take the melody into the lower voices of the orchestra. The short running figures continue around them, and they keep going when Mahler varies the tune.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 86, rehearsal 32: bassoon and cello phrases after the descending orchestral figures. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Scherzo and the fish-sermon song
cues.text: The scherzo is the fish-sermon song without the voice. The woodwinds play the vocal tune in fragments. The strings keep the song’s continuous semiquaver motion.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: Mahler wrote the song for voice and piano in July 1893 while creating an orchestral version of the same material, which, combined with a trio section, became the symphony’s third movement; the symphony movement leaves out most of the vocal melody, and fragments of the slower tune occasionally emerge, often in the woodwinds, above restless rhythmic motion: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Running sixteenths in the violins: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 82.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Manuscript dates, summer 1893
cues.text: On 8 July 1893 Mahler finished the voice-and-piano manuscript of the fish sermon song. Eight days later he dated the orchestral draft of the scherzo. The orchestral version of the song followed on 1 August.

cues.title: Trio in C major
cues.text: The trio opens in C major. After a rumble in the brass and timpani, piccolo and flute hold a high note over low strings marked sehr wuchtig, very weighty. Horns and trumpets then play a fanfare that refers to the First Symphony, and at Vorwärts the full orchestra enters.
cues.evidence: Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: a rumble in the brass and timpani, then a protracted whistle in the piccolo and flute, heralds the central portion, which begins with a brass fanfare that references the First Symphony: https://usuo.org/explore/2014/11/mahler-2-listening-guide . Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 92 (stopped horns and trumpets, timpani), p. 93, rehearsal 36 (no sharps or flats in the signature; piccolo and flute p sempre on a held high note; divided violas, cellos and basses sehr wuchtig; horns and trumpets offen at the end of the page) and p. 94, rehearsal 37 (Vorwärts, full orchestra).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First-trumpet melody
cues.text: The first trumpet plays a long melody over harp arpeggios and running strings. The other trumpets hold soft harmony around it.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 100: first-trumpet melody, supporting trumpet parts, harp arpeggios and string figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of Tempo I, rehearsal 43
cues.text: At rehearsal 43 the opening tempo returns. Running figures pass through the divided strings while the trumpets hold sustained harmony above them. The long melody ends and the scherzo’s earlier motion resumes.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 105, rehearsal 43: Zum Tempo I zurückkehren, running string figures and sustained trumpet harmony.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening texture
cues.text: The scherzo’s opening texture returns in C minor, with running semiquavers in muted violins, plucked lower strings and a bundle of twigs on the bass drum. At rehearsal 46 the full orchestra enters fortissimo. Rushing runs in the winds and strings follow.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 108 (rehearsal 45: three flats, as at the opening; second violins mit Dämpfer, pizzicato lower strings, Ruthe on the bass drum), p. 109 (rehearsal 46: woodwinds ff, horns offen) and pp. 110–111 (the E♭ clarinet again marked mit Humor, then ff runs through the winds and strings).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: B♭-minor climax
cues.text: The scherzo reaches a B♭-minor climax. Brass chords and percussion play over the running strings. The passage returns at the start of the finale, after the alto’s prayer.
cues.evidence: The B♭-minor climax is described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-3-in-ruhig-fliessender-bewegung-scherzo/ ; its recall opens movement V, as described on the Foundation’s finale page.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the low-string figures
cues.text: Long chords in the winds and brass make a diminuendo. Beneath them, divided cellos and basses take up their quick figures again, and stopped horns add a pinched sound.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 118, rehearsal 51: diminuendo, stopped horns and the return of low-string figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ritardando before rehearsal 53
cues.text: The scherzo slows by imperceptible degrees. Muted trumpets and soft woodwind chords hold above a timpani roll. Horns and trumpets play a quiet phrase that the violins take up, molto espressivo, and both harps play an upward glissando.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, pp. 118–122: Wieder unmerklich zurückhaltend (p. 118, rehearsal 51); timpani roll at ppp and trumpets Immer mit Dämpfer (p. 120, rehearsal 52, Immer noch unmerklich zurückhaltend, Zeit lassen); a quiet horn and trumpet phrase and first violins molto espress., lang gestrichen (pp. 120–121); both harps in glissando, with morendo (p. 122, rehearsal 53).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ending and transition to Urlicht
cues.text: At rehearsal 54 the woodwind play rushing scales, ff, above a falling harp glissando. Tempo I returns with the running strings, which thin out over the last pages until only pizzicato strings and a stroke on the tam-tam remain. Mahler directs that the fourth movement follows without any break.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 124 (rehearsal 54: ff woodwind runs, a falling harp glissando marked unisono, Tempo I) and p. 127 (pizzicato strings, a tam-tam stroke in the last bar, and the printed direction Folgt ohne jede Unterbrechung der 4. Satz).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Bassoons and cellos at rehearsal 32
transitions.from: A · Timpani strokes and running string figures
transitions.how: Descending figures pass down through the winds and strings. At rehearsal 32 the bassoons and cellos begin a low, quieter phrase, supported by the horns, with continued movement beneath. The middle section grows out of this thinning of the scherzo texture.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister full score (1897), movement III, p. 86, rehearsal 32.

transitions.title: Held trumpets over returning strings
transitions.to: A′ · Strings resume the opening figures
transitions.how: Mahler writes Zum Tempo I zurückkehren, returning to the first tempo. The trumpets hold chords while short figures return in the divided strings, beginning low and spreading upwards.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 105, rehearsal 43.

transitions.title: The B♭-minor climax
transitions.from: A′ · Strings resume the opening figures
transitions.to: Dev · B♭-minor climax, brass and percussion
transitions.how: Rapid string figures crescendo into a B♭-minor climax for the full orchestra. Winds and brass broaden into emphatic chords, and percussion reinforces the bass. The running accompaniment continues within a much slower, heavier statement.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, pp. 115–118; B♭-minor climax identified at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-3-in-ruhig-fliessender-bewegung-scherzo/

transitions.title: Low strings beneath diminishing brass chords
transitions.from: Dev · B♭-minor climax, brass and percussion
transitions.to: Coda · Cellos and basses resume the motion
transitions.how: The brass and wind chords lengthen and diminish. Stopped horns hold above the quick figures, which return in divided cellos and basses. At rehearsal 51 Mahler marks the passage Wieder unmerklich zurückhaltend, and the lower strings take up the scherzo’s motion again.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 118: Wieder unmerklich zurückhaltend and rehearsal 51, with stopped horns and low-string figures.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, full score (Hofmeister 1897; Weinberger/Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Third movement, pp. 80–127: opening timpani and strings, trumpet song on p. 100, return at rehearsal 43 and the late orchestral outcry.

timeline.note: Timpani strike G and C before the running figures begin.
Strings circle beneath woodwind interjections; a bundle of twigs strikes the bass drum’s wooden shell.
Bassoons and cellos take the melody into the lower orchestra while the small figures continue.
A trumpet plays a broad melody over harp arpeggios and running strings.
Short string figures return beneath held brass and wind notes.
Brass, winds and percussion sound the outcry above the running strings.
Long wind and brass chords fade while cellos and basses resume their quick figures.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
